Give me a comprehensive report, including concerns, architectural issues, Rust semantic and best practices smells, bugs, etc. Be comprehensive. Come at this from a principal engineer lens worried about our v1 release and worried about proving the value of caliper over RDT

I’ll review the last week of changes and open PRs, then trace the highest-risk areas through the architecture, tests, and release goals. I’ll separate verified defects from design risks and gaps in evidence. I’m using the repository’s history-search and audit guidance for this review.

content.text: Two release-facing gaps are emerging. The new wrapper detector infers components from call shape without checking the callee’s signature, so its reported recall needs a precision check. Watch mode also still publishes state through separate containers; I found paths where a snapshot can lose or mix diagnostics and component state. I’m validating these against the final stacked tip and the existing tests before ranking them.

content.text:
# Caliper v1 review

**My release assessment: the project has a credible speed advantage and much better structural coverage than it had a week ago, but the current open stack is not yet a v1 quality gate.** I would continue the staged releases in the [roadmap](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/docs/projects/architecture-roadmap.md), while treating watch correctness, detection precision, and a reproducible RDT comparison as required evidence before calling the output dependable for v1.

I reviewed the 20 PRs merged since October 14, all 20 PRs open on October 21, the final stacked branch, architecture and ADRs, tests, CI, and release workflow. This was a code and CI review; I did not run a new local build or benchmark. The working tree already contains uncommitted changes, which I left untouched. Entire transcript search could not read its saved Keychain login, so the retrospective relies on commits, PRs, and repository documents.

## What the week accomplished

The merged work renamed and published the Caliper packages, changed package metadata and licensing, updated dependencies, separated large inline Rust test modules, added architecture tripwires, and tightened production lints. The open stack then addresses real defects: deterministic enum selection, unreadable files, diagnostic codes, generic `Pick`/`Omit`, barrel resolution, watch parity, and several missed component declaration shapes. These are substantive improvements, and CI is green across the dependent stack.

The measured direction is promising. The [roadmap’s latest source-only comparison](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/docs/projects/architecture-roadmap.md) reports component recall against RDT of 93% for Mantine, 92% for Chakra, 97% for Ant Design, 98% for shadcn/ui, and 99% for react-spectrum after #69. Those numbers establish progress on *recall in that sample*. They do not yet establish precision, output equivalence with dependencies installed, or v1 reliability under incremental updates.

## Findings ranked for release

| Priority | Finding and evidence | Consequence and action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **P0** | **The new wrapper rule can emit non-components.** [#62](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/62) accepts a PascalCase binding when a generic call has a plausible first argument, including any string or identifier; it does not inspect the callee’s return type. A local interface or a type ending in `Props` is enough to select props ([wrapper.rs, lines 43–55 and 105–120](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/extractor/wrapper.rs#L43-L120)). For example, a `Button` constant returned as a string by `makeLabel<ButtonProps>("button")` meets these conditions. | This can inflate recall and pollute consumer output. Before enabling this rule as a default v1 behavior, run the roadmap’s per-family, hand-labeled precision gate, add representative non-component calls, and prefer callee evidence where available. |
| **P0** | **Watch snapshots can combine different revisions.** [#67](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/67) repairs several parity bugs, but `global`, reverse dependencies, named types, components, and diagnostics still publish separately. `update_file` swaps `global`, then independently updates the other stores ([watch.rs, lines 180–212 and 241–301](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L180-L301)); `snapshot()` reads them separately ([lines 129–150](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L129-L150)). Concurrent updates can also load a `global` revision other than the one whose named-type index a call just patched. | HMR consumers can observe stale or mixed props and diagnostics. Implement the documented immutable `WatchRevision` publication model, then test concurrent old-or-new complete snapshots and clean/incremental equivalence. Serializing updates is a reasonable interim containment measure. |
| **P1, confirmed by control flow** | **Initial watch diagnostics disappear from later snapshots.** `initialize()` receives `output` from cold extraction and seeds `component_cache`, but never seeds `self.diagnostics`; `snapshot()` reads only that map plus enum diagnostics ([watch.rs, lines 110–150](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L110-L150)). | A cold parse or I/O error is returned once and then absent from `watch --out` snapshots until an update replaces it. Add an exact initial-output versus snapshot diagnostic test and persist the cold diagnostics. |
| **P1, confirmed by control flow** | **The Vite virtual module retains removed or renamed components.** On HMR, the plugin only assigns `updatedComponents` into `currentOutput.components`; it has no removal path ([index.ts, lines 175–184](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/packages/vite-plugin/src/index.ts#L175-L184)). Rust #67 evicts a changed file’s old cache keys, but the incremental payload does not convey those removals. | A renamed `Card` can leave `Card` beside `Panel` in the virtual module. Return removed keys or a file-scoped replacement and test rename, deletion, and a component that stops resolving. |
| **P1, confirmed by control flow** | **A recorded wrapper candidate can vanish without a diagnostic.** `try_record_wrapper_call` returns `true`, preventing the normal skip diagnostic. During promotion, `select_wrapper_props` returning `None` simply continues ([wrapper.rs, lines 60–89](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/extractor/wrapper.rs#L60-L89)). | This breaks the project rule that degradation is diagnosed. Emit a positioned diagnostic for a rejected recorded candidate, with care to avoid flooding users with ordinary non-components. |
| **P1, semantic defect** | **#69 substitutes generic parameter names inside quoted text.** Its `substitute_identifiers` scans identifier characters without tracking TypeScript string literals ([chain.rs in #69](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/69/files)). For `interface Wrap<T> extends Pick<Base, "T">`, substituting `T = number` also changes the key string `"T"` to `"number"`. | This can select the wrong inherited props while appearing resolved. Substitute on `CollectedType` nodes, as the roadmap already calls for, or at minimum make the temporary parser quote-aware and add this exact regression. |
| **P1, release evidence** | **The RDT advantage is not yet proved end to end.** The new [shape test](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/148bf3ab/crates/core/tests/shapes.rs) checks exact component and prop *names* on synthetic cases. It does not gate corpus precision, types, required flags, defaults, diagnostics, dependency-installed projects, or latency. `just recall` in the roadmap is not implemented. Existing [benchmarks.md](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/c32772ff/docs/benchmarks.md) is dated July and reports different figures and old package names from the October README. | Make one versioned, reproducible scorecard for the five corpora: recall, precision, exact prop fields, degradations, wall time, peak memory, and clean/watch parity. State the hardware, dependency state, tool versions, and comparison mode beside every claim. |

### Architectural issues

1. **The semantic model is still partly text.** `ComponentMapping` and `ExtendsRef` carry type arguments as strings; #69 adds a parser that reconstructs unions, intersections, arrays, and generic references from display text. This improves cases now but preserves the failure class behind D1 and creates a second TypeScript grammar in the resolver. Complete roadmap item 2.1, `Vec<CollectedType>`, before building more wrapper and backend behavior on this path. [#69](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/69)

2. **Detection provenance is partial.** [#60](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/60) adds `DetectionRule`, but classification still uses a first-success `Option` chain and a later wrapper promotion pass ([visit.rs, lines 229–261](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/extractor/visit.rs#L229-L261)). There is no common typed `Detection { Component, Skip, NotCandidate }` contract yet. That makes rule precedence, declined candidates, and diagnostics harder to reason about as more shapes are added.

3. **ADR 0007 needs a precise merge contract.** [ADR 0007](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/docs/adr/0007-backend-discovers-components-and-compiles-in.md) says a structural entry wins on a discovery clash; [ADR 0006](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/c32772ff/docs/adr/0006-semantic-backend-as-second-resolver.md) and the backend design say semantic props replace incomplete structural props. These can coexist only if “discovery clash” and “prop completion” are distinct operations. Define that distinction and its tests before wiring the backend. Likewise, `schemaVersion` should identify the output contract; use separate provenance to tell consumers which backend ran.

4. **A layering back edge remains.** The resolver still imports `pipeline::HtmlAttributeMode` ([resolver/mod.rs, line 142](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/resolver/mod.rs#L142)), contrary to the stated crate/module direction and roadmap 2.3. Move resolver configuration into the shared types boundary before adding backend merge logic.

5. **Watch performance lacks a current gate.** Every update clones `GlobalSourceData` inside `ArcSwap::rcu` ([watch.rs, lines 186–190](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L186-L190)), rebuilds reverse dependencies, and constructs a resolution context. It may be acceptable at today’s corpus size, but the claimed roughly 2 ms edit path needs measurement after the fixes and on large dependency-installed projects. Profile allocation and peak memory before changing data structures.

### Rust, security, and maintainability

- The stronger lint and architecture tests are good safeguards. I did not find evidence of a production `unwrap()` violation in the reviewed stack. There is a small consistency miss: an internal `std::collections::HashMap` remains in pipeline collection where project rules call for `FxHashMap` ([pipeline/mod.rs, line 379](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/mod.rs#L379)).
- The tests added for watch parity compare components and enums in their `visible()` helper, omitting diagnostics ([watch/tests.rs, lines 949–952](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch/tests.rs#L949-L952)). That omission is directly relevant to the initial-diagnostics defect.
- The real Vite/native integration tests are designed to skip when no locally built `.node` file exists. CI’s `test-ts` recipe runs the plugin unit suite; green CI therefore does not prove the real binding and plugin operate together on the release artifacts. Run those integration tests against a built native addon in at least one CI lane.
- I found **no confirmed exploitable security vulnerability** in this review. The exposed inputs still deserve a release-specific robustness gate: malformed TS, cache decoding, process framing, and package install behavior. The roadmap’s proposed property/fuzz work was deferred by [#53](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/53); its golden cache layout test guards format changes, not arbitrary malformed data.
- Documentation drift is now a DX issue. `docs/STATUS.md` still says September and “fully tested”; the architecture notes still describe some already-fixed watch behavior; `MIGRATING.md` and `docs/benchmarks.md` retain the old name. A user comparing Caliper with RDT should encounter one current set of commands and claims.

## All outstanding PRs

The **18 PRs from #52 to #70 are a dependent stack**, so their green checks validate each proposed head against its named parent branch; they are not 18 independently mergeable changes to `main`.

| PRs | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| [#52](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/52), [#53](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/53), [#54](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/54) | Useful foundations: MSRV/SemVer gate, cache byte guard, and parenthesis/non-null detection. #53 is narrower than the roadmap’s proposed property and fuzz gate. |
| [#56](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/56), [#57](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/57), [#58](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/58) | Worth landing as correctness work: deterministic enums, I/O reporting, and clearer codes. Check cache-version and diagnostic compatibility together. |
| [#59](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/59), [#60](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/60), [#61](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/61) | Builders and typed function detection reduce duplication and improve recall. Detection classification and provenance remain incomplete; add negative fixtures for PascalCase helpers. |
| [#62](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/62) | Highest-risk new behavior in the stack. Require measured precision and the missing rejection diagnostic before making its output a v1 claim. |
| [#63](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/63), [#64](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/64), [#65](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/65) | Barrel and utility-type work addresses real missing props; #64 records improved measurements. Re-run against installed dependencies and exact fields. #65 should ultimately share structured arguments with #69. |
| [#66](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/66), [#67](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/67), [#68](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/68) | Removing dead options fixes misleading DX. #67 closes several known watch defects but does not establish coherent revision publication. #68 adds useful exact-name fixtures, not the proposed recall harness. |
| [#69](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/69), [#70](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/70) | #69 materially improves generic and barrel handling, with the string-substitution defect above. #70 records the backend direction; resolve merge precedence, trigger observability, and provenance before implementation. |
| [#46](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/46) | Separate 0.2.2 release PR, with no PR checks shown. Its merge triggers the publish workflow. Review the exact package/version manifest and release run independently of the feature stack. |
| [#44](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/44) | Separate Dependabot PR. CI is red: lint fails because five archived Markdown files fail `oxfmt`. Hold it until that check passes; the failure is formatting, not a Rust test failure. |

None of the open PRs showed a recorded review decision in the GitHub metadata I retrieved. All checks shown for #52–#70 were successful; that is useful evidence, but the missing product and concurrency gates above remain.

## Recommended v1 sequence

1. **Land the correctness stack in order**, with focused fixes for #69’s quoted-key substitution and #62’s rejected-candidate diagnostic and false-positive gate.
2. **Make watch output coherent**, then verify exact components, props, enums, diagnostics, rename/removal behavior, and concurrent snapshots against cold extraction. Include the Vite virtual module in that gate.
3. **Publish a reproducible Caliper-versus-RDT scorecard.** Lead with accuracy and precision at a stated mode, then speed and memory for the same projects. Keep the structural default and opt-in checker results separate.
4. **Finish the type-argument and detection contracts** before integrating the TypeScript backend. Settle ADR 0007’s merge and provenance rules first.
5. **Run release-artifact tests and refresh user docs** before labeling v1: native addon plus Vite integration, platform package installation, current CLI/API guides, and one maintained benchmark page.

Caliper’s strongest value proposition is already visible: fast structural extraction with useful diagnostics and incremental access. For v1, the decisive proof is that those advantages survive real library shapes, false-positive review, file edits, and packaged installation with results a user can reproduce.

Claude has been pushing a hell of a lot of PRs and I'm worried that we're doing a lot of one-of cases chasing the numbers from RDT vs thinking through our oxc architecture and ts 7.1 plans on how to actually adopt things appropriately.

Can you take a look at all of work. Do another round of analysis as before plus the concerns above?

This is what claude itself said:

On AST and typing vs special cases: it's a mix. The core is structural, but a layer of name-based rules sits around it.

Decided from structure:
- What counts as a component: JSX, hooks or the shape of what it returns (#71), not library names.
- Wrapper props: read from the call's type arguments and payload type, not from a list of wrapper names.
- Type arguments and key sets: type arguments are typed values (the old string parsers are gone), and Pick/Omit keys are computed from those types.
- Everything from this round (#75–#82) is general machinery and adds no special cases:
  - watch revisions with recorded dependencies
  - one entry per diagnostic
  - the cache fingerprint
  - the speed-ups
  - streamed JSON output
  - generic-alias substitution, which on its own cut leaked parameter names on Mantine from 25,624 to 72

Still decided by name (a count of string-literal name checks per file):

┌────────────────────────┬───────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Where          │ Count │                                             What it is                                              │
├────────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ react_types.rs         │   218 │ React built-ins and HTML attribute tables                                                           │
├────────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ known.rs               │    55 │ Shortcuts for libraries: SxProps, VariantProps, cva, tv, Panda                                      │
├────────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ resolver/named.rs      │    14 │ A list of names to leave unexpanded silently, e.g. HTMLAttributes, or anything starting HTML and    │
│                        │       │ ending Element                                                                                      │
├────────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ extractor/component.rs │    13 │ Renaming wrappers spotted by callee name: memo, observer, names containing "forwardref" or          │
│                        │       │ "Component", with[A-Z]                                                                              │
├────────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Built-in utility types │     — │ Omit, Pick, Partial, Required, PropsWithChildren are each handled by name; mapped and conditional   │
│                        │       │ types fall back to "opaque"                                                                         │
└────────────────────────┴───────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Some of this is fair, because there's no type checker: React and the TypeScript lib types are a fixed vocabulary. Most of it could be structural instead:
1. The silence list becomes "the name is declared in a TypeScript lib or @types file". We already load those files.
2. The wrapper-name rules become "the argument shows render evidence", which the generic wrapper path already does.
3. The library shortcuts move behind the DocgenPlugin hook, so the core holds no library names.
4. A small evaluator for keyof and mapped types over a known, finite set of keys replaces the per-name utility handling. It would also cover Record and many of the remaining opaque types.
5. The React tables come from @types/react when it's installed.

I’ll re-review the full PR stack, with a specific test for your concern: which changes improve Caliper’s semantic model and which only improve a benchmark case. I’ll also check Claude’s claims against the code, look at how the work fits the OXC and TypeScript 7.1 boundaries, and update the release risks from the first review.

content.text: I found a concrete watch delta bug that the snapshot parity tests miss: when duplicate component names change their output keys, the full snapshot is rebuilt correctly, but the incremental event omits a surviving component whose key moved. I’m folding that into the release assessment alongside the remaining detector and type resolution risks.

# Caliper v1 review — October 21, 2026

**My assessment: the work is moving toward the stated architecture, but I would not treat the current PR stack as v1 ready.** Claude’s “mix” description is fair. The recent changes replace several brittle mechanisms with structured data and fix real watch and cache defects. The remaining risk is that Caliper can still emit a plausible component or prop type from a name heuristic without knowing what that symbol means. That is more damaging to trust than a diagnosed omission.

I reviewed the current branch tips, PR descriptions and CI, the architecture roadmap and ADRs, and the relevant extractor, resolver, watch, serialization, and Vite paths. I did not change the working tree or run a fresh corpus benchmark. The repository’s Entire session-history search was unavailable because its Keychain access failed, so the historical account below comes from Git and PR evidence.

## What changed, and what the PR queue means

There are **27 open PRs**: 25 chained PRs from [#58](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/58) through [#82](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/82), the [0.2.2 release PR #46](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/46), and [Dependabot #84](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/84). [#57](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/57) and [#83](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/83) merged during this review. The #82 tip has green CI; #84 currently fails lint. Several lower PRs have queued or absent checks, so the green tip is useful evidence for the combined branch, not a substitute for testing the final merge on `main`.

| Work | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| [#58–#60](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/60), [#68](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/68) | Better diagnostic vocabulary, recorded detection rules, and exact per-shape component/prop tests. Good foundations; the detection model is still spread across rules. |
| [#61–#63](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/62), [#69](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/69) | Meaningful gains for typed functions, wrapper calls, generic interfaces, and barrels. Wrapper detection remains an inference from arguments and names, rather than callee return semantics. |
| [#65](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/65), [#72–#74](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/73), [#82](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/82) | The strongest semantic progress: structured type arguments, key-set evaluation, and generic substitution. These address causes of incorrect output, not just corpus-specific counts. |
| [#66–#67](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/67), [#75–#78](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/75) | Removed misleading options and substantially repaired watch parity, atomic snapshots, Vite refresh, and diagnostic aggregation. The incremental **delta** contract still has a defect described below. |
| [#79–#81](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/81) | Build-aware cache invalidation and measured resolver/serialization improvements. The streaming serializer has a strong byte-equivalence test. |
| [#70](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/70) | Useful TypeScript 7.1 beta probe and ADR. The checker is still **not connected** to core, CLI, or NAPI. |

This also corrects several findings from my prior review: the text-based type-argument parser is gone; watch publishes an atomic revision; the Vite virtual module reads the session snapshot; and an unresolved wrapper no longer vanishes merely because it has zero resolved props. Those fixes deserve credit.

## Release-significant findings

### 1. Name-based resolution can override a real local type — high

The resolver checks bare React builtin names **before** looking up a source declaration. A project-local `ReactNode`, `CSSProperties`, or `Ref` can therefore be classified as React’s type instead of the project’s type. In the props-chain path, TypeScript utility recognition likewise happens before source lookup; a locally declared `Partial` or `Required` can be treated as a utility and yield an empty chain. The later “source before known pattern” rule does not protect these earlier exits. This is a direct symbol-identity bug, not a philosophical objection to tables. See [`named.rs`](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/crates/core/src/resolver/named.rs#L68-L79) and [`chain.rs`](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/crates/core/src/resolver/chain.rs#L65-L83).

**Fix before v1:** resolve the binding first. Apply a builtin interpretation only when its origin is known, or as an explicit fallback when resolution fails; report that fallback.

### 2. “Render evidence” is useful, but weaker than the claim made for it — high

[#71](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/71) reduces false positives. Its implementation still accepts JSX **anywhere** in a function body, including a nested callback or an expression never returned. It also accepts a returned `null`, a call whose spelling begins with a capital letter or `use`, and an element-like return annotation by its rightmost name, without resolving the symbol. A typed `FormatName` that constructs unused JSX and returns a string can pass the detector. A custom imported type named `ReactNode` can pass the return-annotation check. See [`evidence.rs`](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/crates/core/src/extractor/evidence.rs#L16-L157).

The wrapper path additionally treats a PascalCase argument as a component and chooses a props argument because it is declared locally or ends in `Props`; it does **not** establish that the callee returns a component. The rename path still accepts `memo`, `observer`, names containing `Component` or `forwardref`, `withX`, and any curried call. See [`wrapper.rs`](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/crates/core/src/extractor/wrapper.rs#L81-L197) and [`component.rs`](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/crates/core/src/extractor/component.rs#L569-L586).

This matters because [#62 explicitly turned the roadmap’s default-off guessing tier on](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/62) based largely on a Mantine comparison. [#71’s later measurements](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/71) report 109 Ant Design and 233 Spectrum entries beyond RDT. Those are **not automatically false positives**—RDT is an imperfect oracle—but they have not been hand-labeled to satisfy the roadmap’s 95% precision gate per family. I would hold further detector expansion until that gate exists.

### 3. The watch snapshot is correct in cases where its incremental event is wrong — high

[#75](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/75) tests that a full snapshot matches a cold extraction after edits. The delta is assembled only from freshly resolved components. Consider two components named `X` in different files. Delete the file whose `X` held the bare key: the surviving, **kept** component moves from `X (file)` to `X`, but is absent from `updatedComponents`. The event removes `X (file)` while the old `X` remains in a client applying the documented delta. Creating an earlier same-named component produces the inverse loss. The complete virtual-module reload can mask this for one Vite consumer; the public event contract remains wrong. The same delta carries current diagnostics but no explicit removals for diagnostics that disappeared. See [`Revision::next`](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/crates/core/src/pipeline/revision.rs#L316-L361) and the [Vite event contract](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/packages/vite-plugin/src/index.ts#L18-L26).

Add tests that apply every emitted delta to the prior output and compare the result with `snapshot()`, including name collisions, diagnostic disappearance, and two different files updating concurrently. The Vite plugin guards ordering per file; an older update from another file can still be sent after a newer revision.

### 4. The semantic-backend contract has an unresolved contradiction — high

[ADR 0007](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/docs/adr/0007-backend-discovers-components-and-compiles-in.md) says a structural entry wins on a clash. The [integration design](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/docs/type-checker-integration.md) says checker props replace structural props. That distinction may mean “structural identity wins, checker props may replace,” but the merge contract does not say so. It must specify component identity, field-level precedence, diagnostic retirement, provenance, and what happens when the checker and OXC disagree.

The proposed trigger is also incomplete: it includes “a callee-added prop [the structural pass] cannot see,” yet there is no way for the structural pass to flag an unseen prop. Bare generic names and silent terminal types also avoid degradation diagnostics. Triggering only on visible incompleteness will miss precisely some cases the checker is meant to repair. Finally, `schemaVersion` should identify the **wire schema**, not whether discovery ran; mode and provenance need separate fields.

The official [TypeScript 7.1 beta announcement](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-1-beta/) now documents `typescript/sync`, `/async`, and `/fs`. Caliper’s beta smoke test is timely, but its own [integration document](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/docs/type-checker-integration.md) says full beta parity, Rust-client cost, large-project behavior, and several lifecycle gates remain open. I would settle the merge contract before adding more structural guesses.

### 5. Silent or lossy output remains in named shortcuts — medium to high

The “silent no-op” list leaves utility, DOM, and HTML names unexpanded by spelling, even when their actual declaration or provenance has not been established. `known.rs` maps React Aria `RenderProps` to scalar `className` and `style` props while deliberately omitting a function-valued form; that can misdescribe a consumer’s accepted values without an opacity diagnostic. See [`named.rs`](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/crates/core/src/resolver/named.rs#L131-L174) and [`known.rs`](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/crates/core/src/known.rs#L108-L137).

A separate, older path parses `tsconfig.json` aliases with a hand-written line-comment stripper; block comments or read/parse failure result in no aliases and no diagnostic. That is a common configuration shape and violates the project’s stated “diagnose degradation” rule. See [`react.rs`](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/crates/core/src/resolver/react.rs#L153-L205).

### 6. Performance and resource gates need to be applied to the finished feature — medium

[#80](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/80) and [#81](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/81) show convincing gains. [#82](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/82) then increases Mantine’s measured run from **90 to 112 ms** and output size by **23%** while fixing generic types. That may be a good trade, but it crosses the roadmap’s proposed “15 ms or 20%” regression gate relative to its immediate predecessor. The “25,624 leaked parameter-name leaves to 72” result is strong evidence that substitution is working; it is **not** a prop-accuracy or end-user correctness metric.

Watch edits now clone the global source/index state and reassemble every output component, including rerunning component plugin hooks, even when only one component is resolved again. [#75’s own measurements](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/75) show a Mantine leaf edit rising from 8.3 to 13.5 ms. This is a reasonable correctness-first design, but it needs a large-project latency and memory gate before “fast incremental” becomes a v1 promise. The dependency recorder is thread-local and implicit, so a new resolver lookup can silently omit an invalidation edge unless tested.

For security and robustness, the [DTS cache loader](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/crates/core/src/cache.rs#L153-L189) reads and deserializes the entire local cache before applying any entry bound. A malformed or oversized cache can consume substantial memory. I found no basis to call this a remote exploit; it is a resource bound to add if CI or user workspaces may contain untrusted cache files.

## How I would handle Claude’s five proposals

| Proposal | Recommendation |
| --- | --- |
| Replace silence list with “declared in lib or `@types`” | **Use symbol origin, but do not make every dependency declaration terminal.** Many `@types` aliases are precisely what Caliper should follow. Record why resolution stopped. |
| Replace wrapper names with argument render evidence | **Insufficient alone.** Arguments can be components while the callee returns a string, config, or context. Use callee declaration/signature when structural data permits; otherwise label the result inferred and measure precision. |
| Move library shortcuts to `DocgenPlugin` | **Requires a new boundary.** Today’s plugin hooks run after file extraction or after a component is resolved; they cannot decide a type during resolution. Define a version-aware type-resolution adapter/preset before moving these rules. |
| Add a finite `keyof`/mapped-type evaluator | **Yes, within a budget.** #73 is a good start. Specify supported finite operations, depth/cost limits, and an opaque diagnostic for unknown keys. Avoid gradually implementing a second TypeScript checker. |
| Read React tables from installed `@types/react` | **Use installed declarations where requested and available, with a curated fallback.** A blanket dependency would make the fast default vary with installed React versions and package layout. Binding identity must be fixed first. |

## What would prove Caliper’s value over RDT

The strongest case is **fast structural extraction with useful typed output, explicit degradation, and reliable incremental updates**, plus an opt-in checker for the cases structural analysis cannot answer. Raw component counts alone do not prove that case. The roadmap currently mixes “own props,” “any props,” source-only mirrors, and different baselines; [#71](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/71) itself reports 87% Mantine and 80% Chakra `recall(any)` while the [roadmap](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/docs/projects/architecture-roadmap.md) highlights higher own-prop figures. Publish one reproducible scorecard with both measures, hand-labeled precision, prop type/required/default/description agreement, diagnostics, wall time, peak RSS, and watch parity. Run it with dependencies installed as well as on source-only mirrors.

The comparison should keep RDT’s actual output as a compatibility oracle, while separately marking RDT mistakes and product-policy differences. The existing [benchmark document](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/docs/benchmarks.md) dates to July and the [status page](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/1bae571b/docs/STATUS.md) to September; both need a current, reconciled release claim. TypeScript 7’s native checker and 7.1 API make the long-term speed comparison a moving target, so the structured output, diagnostics, and dependable watch contract matter as much as the multiplier.

## Recommended decision

1. **Keep the structural fixes and measured serializer improvements.** They are substantive, and #82’s substitution addresses a real semantic error.
2. **Block a v1 readiness claim** on symbol precedence, delta reconstruction, a hand-labeled detector precision gate, and the semantic merge/trigger contract.
3. **Freeze new library shortcuts and wrapper heuristics** until those gates show which gaps genuinely require them.
4. **Land the stack in reviewable cohorts**, then run CI and the complete corpus on the resulting `main`. Treat [#46](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/46) as a separate publishing decision: merging it publishes packages. Resolve [#84’s](https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/84) lint failure independently.

The core concern is justified, but the direction is recoverable: the newest PRs contain genuine architecture work. The v1 risk is allowing the remaining guesses and comparison numbers to stand in for a precise contract about what Caliper knows, infers, and cannot yet resolve.
